claim: Cilia are hairlike organelles involved in both sensory functions and motility.
source: Cilia are hairlike organelles involved in both sensory functions and motility.
evidence: This is a general statement about cilia that draws from established scientific knowledge about their structure and function.

claim: A non-motile cilium in a quiescent fluid has a capture rate equivalent to a circular absorbing region with approximately 4 times its surface area.
source: Because of its geometry, a non-motile cilium in a quiescent fluid has a capture rate equivalent to a circular absorbing region with ∼4× its surface area.
evidence: This claim is supported by analytical calculations and simulations presented in the manuscript, specifically in the Results section on 'Cilium in quiescent fluid' and shown in Figure 2.

claim: When a cilium is exposed to an external shear flow, the equivalent surface area increases to approximately 6 times its actual surface area.
source: When the cilium is exposed to an external shear flow, the equivalent surface area increases to ∼6×.
evidence: This claim is supported by analytical calculations and numerical simulations for cilia in shear flow, presented in the Results section and Figure 2.

claim: If a cilium beats in a non-reciprocal way in an otherwise quiescent fluid, its capture rate increases with the beating frequency to the power of 1/3.
source: Alternatively, if the cilium beats in a non-reciprocal way in an otherwise quiescent fluid, its capture rate increases with the beating frequency to the power of 1/3.
evidence: This claim is supported by numerical simulations of beating cilia shown in Figure 3, where the capture rate scales as Pe^(1/3) at high Péclet numbers.

claim: Cilia are found on most eukaryotic cells.
source: They are found on most eukaryotic cells (Nachury and Mick, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nachury and Mick, 2019.

claim: Primary cilia have primarily sensory functions.
source: Primary cilia, of which there is only one on each cell, have primarily sensory functions (as receptors for chemical, mechanical, or other signals) (Zimmermann, 1898; Berbari et al., 2009; Hilgendorf et al., 2016; Spasic and Jacobs, 2017; Ferreira et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the scientific literature.

claim: Primary cilia are often referred to as 'the cell's antenna' due to their shape and role in signalling.
source: Due to their shape and their role in signalling, they are often referred to as 'the cell's antenna' (Marshall and Nonaka, 2006; Malicki and Johnson, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marshall and Nonaka, 2006 and Malicki and Johnson, 2017.

claim: Motile cilia move the surrounding fluid by beating in an asymmetric fashion.
source: Motile cilia, typically appearing in larger numbers (Brooks and Wallingford, 2014; Spassky and Meunier, 2017), move the surrounding fluid by beating in an asymmetric fashion (Golestanian et al., 2011; Gilpin et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the scientific literature.

claim: Primary cilia in the vertebrate left-right organiser are motile and drive a lateral fluid flow.
source: Primary cilia in the vertebrate left-right organiser are motile and drive a lateral fluid flow that triggers, through a mechanism that is not yet fully understood, a distinct signalling cascade determining the body laterality (Essner et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Essner et al., 2002.

claim: There is mounting evidence that motile cilia can have various sensory roles.
source: There is also mounting evidence that motile cilia can have various sensory roles (Bloodgood, 2010), including chemical reception (Shah et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bloodgood, 2010 and Shah et al., 2009.

claim: Receptors localised on motile cilia, such as ACE2, can act as entry points for viruses including SARS-CoV-2.
source: Adversely, receptors localised on motile cilia, such as ACE2, can also act as entry points for viruses including SARS-CoV-2 (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2020.

claim: Some chemosensory systems are known to achieve a sensitivity high enough to detect a small number of molecules.
source: Some chemosensory systems, including vomeronasal (Leinders-Zufall et al., 2000) and olfactory neurons (Bhandawat et al., 2010) and marine sperm cells (Kaupp et al., 2003), are known to achieve a sensitivity high enough to detect a small number of molecules.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on different chemosensory systems.

claim: Only 1% of the surface area of a cell or cilium needs to be covered in high-affinity receptors to obtain near-perfect adsorption.
source: Because diffusion is fast on very short length scales, only 1% of the surface area of a cell or cilium needs to be covered in high-affinity receptors to obtain near-perfect adsorption (Berg and Purcell, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berg and Purcell, 1977.

claim: Flagella-driven swimming microorganisms can break the diffusion limit to increase their access to nutrients.
source: In either of these cases, as long as there is no advection, the binding rates can be estimated using the theory of diffusion-limited reactions (Adam and Delbruck, 1968). This binding rate is known as the diffusion limit, and it has already been shown that flagella-driven swimming microorganisms can break the diffusion limit in order to increase their access to nutrients (Short et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Short et al., 2006.

claim: Placing receptors on a cilium forms a compartment that facilitates efficient accumulation of second messengers.
source: Because of its small volume, a cilium forms a compartment that facilitates efficient accumulation of second messengers (Marshall and Nonaka, 2006; Hilgendorf et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marshall and Nonaka, 2006 and Hilgendorf et al., 2016.

claim: The location of chemoreceptors on cilia exposes them to fluid that is better mixed.
source: It has also been suggested that the location of chemoreceptors on cilia exposes them to fluid that is better mixed (Marshall and Nonaka, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marshall and Nonaka, 2006.

claim: Hydrodynamic interaction between motile and sensory cilia can enhance the sensitivity of sensory cilia.
source: A recent study suggests that the hydrodynamic interaction between motile and sensory cilia can enhance the sensitivity of the latter (Reiten et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reiten et al., 2017.

claim: The ratio of the simulated capture rate to the analytical rate constant for a cilium in quiescent fluid is 1.02.
source: This value agrees well with simulations: the ratio of the simulated to this analytical rate constant is 1.02.
evidence: This claim is supported by numerical simulations that validate the analytical result.

claim: The capture rate of a cilium scales almost linearly with its length.
source: The finding that the capture rate scales almost linearly with the length of the cilium can be compared to experimental data obtained on olfactory cilia from the nasal cavity of mouse, whose lengths in different regions vary from a few micrometers to tens of micrometers.
evidence: This is inferred from the analytical expression for k_cilium and supported by comparison with experimental data.

claim: Olfactory cilia from different regions of the mouse nasal cavity show sensitivity thresholds that differ by an order of magnitude.
source: Challis et al., 2015 have used patch-clamp recordings on olfactory sensory neurons and measured the response to pulses of an odorant (eugenol or a mixture of 10 odorants), lasting 5-400⁢ms. Regions with different lengths show very different sensitivity thresholds, differing by an order of magnitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental data from Challis et al., 2015.

claim: The experimental results on olfactory cilia sensitivity are qualitatively consistent with the predicted length dependence of the capture rate.
source: The results are qualitatively consistent with the predicted length dependence of the capture rate.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the theoretical predictions with experimental data.

claim: For olfactory cilia with lengths from 2.5 μm to 100 μm, the calculated area ratio ranges from 2.7 to 18.
source: If we neglect the fact that long cilia are not straight, the calculated area ratio ranges from 2.7 to 18.
evidence: This is calculated from the analytical expressions for different cilium lengths.

claim: Using an exact numerical result for the capacitance of a cylinder, the area ratio becomes 4.5 for L/a=80.
source: Using an exact numerical result for the capacitance of a cylinder (Paffuti, 2018), the ratio becomes 4.5 for L/a=80.
evidence: This claim uses a more exact numerical result from Paffuti, 2018 to refine the calculation.

claim: At the scale of cilia, the flow is characterised by a low Reynolds number, meaning that viscous forces dominate over inertia.
source: At the scale of cilia, the flow is characterised by a low Reynolds number, meaning that viscous forces dominate over inertia.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of fluid mechanics at microscopic scales.

claim: The capture rate shows a strong positive relationship between cilium length and sensitivity.
source: This expression for the rate once again shows a strong positive relationship between cilium length and sensitivity, as is known to be the case in real biological systems (Challis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the analytical expression and supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: The characteristic Péclet number for the cross-over between diffusive and convective capture is of the order ~L/a ≈ 80.
source: The characteristic Péclet number for the cross-over between the diffusive and the convective capture is of the order ∼L/a≈80.
evidence: This is inferred from the scaling of the capture rate expressions.

claim: A cilium is better per area than a patch at both low and high Péclet numbers, but excels when the Péclet number is large.
source: This means that a cilium is better per area than a patch at both low and high Péclet numbers, but the cilium excels when the Péclet number is large.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the area ratios at different Péclet numbers.

claim: A cilium with receptors over the distal 50% of its length achieves 60% of the maximal capture rate at high Péclet numbers.
source: A cilium with receptors over the distal 50% of its length therefore achieves 60% of the maximal capture rate.
evidence: This is calculated from the modified integration and compared to simulations in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A purely reciprocally moving cilium displays almost no improvement in capture rate over several orders of magnitude of the Péclet number.
source: The reciprocally moving cilium (Figure 3a) displays almost no improvement over several orders of magnitude of the Péclet number.
evidence: This is shown in the numerical simulations presented in Figure 3e.

claim: Purcell's scallop theorem states that purely reciprocal motion does not create any net flow.
source: This is expected, because Purcell's scallop theorem (Purcell, 1977) states that purely reciprocal motion does not create any net flow
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Purcell, 1977.

claim: A cilium moving around a vertical cone shows an increase in rate constant by a factor of two over a few orders of magnitude of the Péclet number.
source: The cilium moving around a vertical cone (Figure 3b) induces a net rotational flow, but no inflow or outflow (by symmetry, the time-averaged flow can only have a rotational component [Vilfan, 2012]). Nevertheless, the constant motion of the cilium through the fluid leads to a higher local capture efficiency. The rate constant therefore shows more improvement; over a few orders of magnitude of the Péclet number, the rate constant increases by a factor of two.
evidence: This is shown in numerical simulations in Figure 3e and explained by the rotational flow pattern.

claim: A cilium moving in a tilted cone induces a long range flow characterized by a finite volume flow rate.
source: When the cilium is near to the plane, the no-slip boundary screens the flow, whereas when it is far from the plane, its pumping is unimpeded. This results in the cilium inducing a long range flow in one direction, characterised by a finite volume flow rate (Smith et al., 2008).
evidence: This is explained by the asymmetry in the cilium's motion and supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2008.

claim: A cilium with a realistic beating pattern has a capture rate close to that of the tilted cone, but surpasses it at very high Péclet numbers.
source: We finally simulated the capture process on a cilium exerting a realistic beating pattern, consisting of a stretched working stroke and a bent, sweeping recovery stroke (Figure 3d). The capture rate is close to that of the tilted cone, but surpasses it at very high Péclet numbers.
evidence: This is shown in the numerical simulations in Figure 3e.

claim: At zero Péclet number, a bundle of cilia has a per-cilium capture rate of approximately 0.5 times that of an isolated cilium.
source: Using numerical simulations, we find that at zero Péclet number (Figure 4a–b), Q≈0.5, which means that the cilia locally deplete the concentration field, harming the per-cilium effectiveness
evidence: This is shown in numerical simulations comparing isolated and bundled cilia at Pe=0.

claim: For motile cilia at Pe≈10000, the per-cilium capture rate in a bundle is around 50% higher than for an isolated cilium.
source: However, when the cilia actively move (with each tracing out a tilted cone with a different randomly-chosen phase lag compared to its neighbours, as in Figure 4e) the trend is reversed: we find that at Pe≈10000, Q≈1.53, meaning that per cilium, the capture rate is around 50% higher in the collective when compared to an isolated cilium with the same Péclet number.
evidence: This is shown in numerical simulations of beating cilium bundles in Figure 4.

claim: Cilia that beat with random phases are more effective than cilia that beat in phase.
source: When comparing these randomly chosen phases to a patch of cilia which beat in uniform, we find that cilia which beat in phase (Figure 4d) see an improvement over the stationary case with Q≈1.16, but are much less effective than the cilia patch that beats with random phases.
evidence: This is shown in numerical simulations comparing uniform and random phase beating in Figure 4.

claim: Random phases give a higher volume flow and complex hydrodynamic interactions result in a slightly higher capture chance.
source: The random phases give a higher volume flow, and complex hydrodynamic interactions between the randomly-phased cilia result in a slightly higher capture chance for any given particle.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results and the observed differences between random and uniform phase beating.

claim: Mutual enhancement of capture rates in cilium bundles is a robust phenomenon that does not depend on a specific geometry.
source: The results suggest that mutual enhancement of capture rates is a robust phenomenon and does not depend on a specific geometry.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulations showing similar improvements for different bundle configurations.

claim: A chemosensory cilium working at the physical limit is capable of detecting picomolar ligand concentrations on a timescale of seconds.
source: A chemosensory cilium working at the physical limit is therefore capable of detecting picomolar ligand concentrations on a timescale of seconds.
evidence: This is inferred from the calculated capture rate constant.

claim: Sensitivity thresholds in the sub-picomolar range have been measured in some olfactory neurons.
source: Sensitivity thresholds in the sub-picomolar range have been measured in some olfactory neurons (Frings and Lindemann, 1990; Zhang et al., 2013), indicating that some olfactory cilia work close to the theoretical sensitivity limit.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental measurements.

claim: With larger molecules and higher viscosities, Péclet numbers can exceed 10^4, leading to significant enhancement of the capture rate.
source: However, with larger molecules and higher viscosities, the Péclet numbers can exceed 104, leading to a significant enhancement of the capture rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the scaling relationships and the effect of viscosity and molecule size on the Péclet number.

claim: When a cilium is beating with a frequency of 25 Hz, the Péclet number is of the order ~10.
source: When the same cilium is beating with a frequency of 25Hz, the Péclet number is of the order ∼10, which is too small to have an effect on the capture rate.
evidence: This is calculated from the cilium dimensions and beating frequency.

claim: With a medium viscosity of 0.2 Pa·s and a Stokes radius of 10 nm, the Péclet number reaches 10^5, meaning motility accelerates the capture rate by one order of magnitude.
source: With a medium viscosity of 0.2Pa⋅s (200 times the water viscosity) and a Stokes radius of 10nm, it reaches 105, meaning that the motility accelerates the capture rate by one order of magnitude.
evidence: This is calculated from the parameters and the scaling relationship for capture rate with Péclet number.

claim: Motile cilia in the zebrafish left-right organizer (Kupffer's vesicle) may both generate flow and detect signalling particles, possibly extracellular vesicles.
source: For example, according to one hypothesis, motile cilia in the zebrafish left-right organizer (Kupffer's vesicle) both generate flow and detect signalling particles, possibly extracellular vesicles (Ferreira et al., 2017; Ferreira et al., 2019) similar to the proposed 'nodal vesicular parcels' (Tanaka et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Ferreira et al., 2017, Ferreira et al., 2019, and Tanaka et al., 2005.

claim: Particle size can have a direct steric effect on the capture rate.
source: However, when the particle size becomes comparable to the cilium diameter, the approximation that treats them as point particles loses validity. Indeed, it has been shown that particle size can have a direct steric effect on the capture rate (Ding and Kanso, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ding and Kanso, 2015.

claim: The capture process of large particles can depend on a competition between hydrodynamic and adhesive forces.
source: Furthermore, the capture process of large particles can depend on a competition between hydrodynamic and adhesive forces (Tripathi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tripathi et al., 2013.

claim: Steric effects can lead to particle enrichment in flow compartments.
source: Steric effects can even lead to particle enrichment in flow compartments (Nawroth et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nawroth et al., 2017.

claim: For individual isolated cilia, the geometry of a cilium always means an advantage in chemical sensitivity over receptors covering the same area on a flat surface.
source: We have thus proven that for individual isolated cilia the geometry of a cilium always means an advantage in chemical sensitivity over receptors covering the same area on a flat surface (assuming they act as perfect absorbers), whether in a quiescent or moving fluid.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analytical and numerical results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: At high Péclet numbers, the advantage of a cilium increases further and confers an advantage in chemosensitivity to cilium bundles over individual cilia.
source: At high Péclet numbers, which are achieved in viscous fluids, with very large particles or in very strong flows, the advantage of a cilium increases further and even confers an advantage in chemosensitivity to cilium bundles over individual cilia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the numerical simulations of cilium bundles at high Péclet numbers.

claim: The hydrodynamics are computed using a modified Rotne-Prager mobility tensor that accounts for the no-slip boundary.
source: The hydrodynamics are computed using a modified Rotne-Prager mobility tensor 𝐌 that accounts for the no-slip boundary.
evidence: This describes the computational method used in the simulations.

claim: In the simulations, N=20 spheres were used, corresponding to an aspect ratio L/a=40.
source: In the simulations we used N=20 spheres, corresponding to an aspect ratio L/a=40.
evidence: This describes a parameter choice in the numerical simulations.

claim: The Rotne-Prager tensor approximation does not exactly satisfy the no-slip boundary condition on the surface of the cilium, especially at high Péclet numbers.
source: The Rotne-Prager tensor approximation used to determine the flow fields does not exactly satisfy the no-slip boundary condition on the surface of the cilium, especially at high Péclet numbers.
evidence: This is a limitation of the computational method acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The elongated shape of a cilium provides an advantage for the capture rate of molecules in the surrounding fluid.
source: Besides the well-known advantages of compartmentalisation, which facilitates the downstream signal processing, we show that the elongated shape of a cilium provides an advantage for the capture rate of molecules in the surrounding fluid.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the analytical and numerical results.

claim: A cilium within an immotile bundle has a lower capture rate than an isolated cilium.
source: Finally, we show that a cilium within an immotile bundle has a lower capture rate than an isolated cilium, but a higher one when the cilia are sufficiently motile.
evidence: This is shown in the numerical simulations comparing isolated and bundled cilia at different Péclet numbers.

claim: A cilium within a motile bundle has a higher capture rate than an isolated cilium when the cilia are sufficiently motile.
source: Finally, we show that a cilium within an immotile bundle has a lower capture rate than an isolated cilium, but a higher one when the cilia are sufficiently motile.
evidence: This is shown in the numerical simulations of beating cilium bundles at high Péclet numbers.

claim: The protruding geometry of a cilium could be one of the reasons why so many receptors are located on cilia.
source: Altogether, our results show that the protruding geometry of a cilium could be one of the reasons why so many receptors are located on cilia.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the demonstrated advantages of ciliary geometry for capture rates.

claim: The results point to the advantage of combining motility with chemical reception.
source: They also point to the advantage of combining motility with chemical reception.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated enhancement of capture rates by ciliary motility.
